claim: The majority of glycan species on OVA correspond to the complex-type (54.9%).
source: We found that the majority of glycan species on OVA corresponded to the complex-type (54.9%), while mannose-rich glycans (mainly Man5 and Man6, potential ligands of the MR (Taylor and Drickamer, 1993)) represented only 23% of all glycoforms (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from normal-phase HPLC coupled with mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mannose-rich glycans (mainly Man5 and Man6) represent 23% of all glycoforms on OVA.
source: We found that the majority of glycan species on OVA corresponded to the complex-type (54.9%), while mannose-rich glycans (mainly Man5 and Man6, potential ligands of the MR (Taylor and Drickamer, 1993)) represented only 23% of all glycoforms (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from glycan profiling analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Hybrid glycoforms represent 16.2% of OVA glycans.
source: The remaining glycoforms were of the hybrid (16.2%) and oligomannose (Man3, 3%) type.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from glycan profiling analysis.

claim: Oligomannose (Man3) glycoforms represent 3% of OVA glycans.
source: The remaining glycoforms were of the hybrid (16.2%) and oligomannose (Man3, 3%) type.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from glycan profiling analysis.

claim: The presence of mannose rich glycans on OVA correlates with earlier reports that MR interacted with OVA.
source: The presence of mannose rich glycans on OVA correlate with the earlier reports that in particular MR interacted with OVA (Burgdorf et al., 2006) and mediated the TLR dependent and TAP-1 dependent cross-presentation of OVA (Burgdorf et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Burgdorf et al., 2006.

claim: MR mediated the TLR dependent and TAP-1 dependent cross-presentation of OVA.
source: The presence of mannose rich glycans on OVA correlate with the earlier reports that in particular MR interacted with OVA (Burgdorf et al., 2006) and mediated the TLR dependent and TAP-1 dependent cross-presentation of OVA (Burgdorf et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Burgdorf et al., 2008.

claim: At least 40% of the total OVA-LeX preparation contained the LeX glycan.
source: Using mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF/TOF), we confirmed that OVA-LeX increases to 1.2 KDa in mass, indicating that at least 40% of the total OVA-LeX preparation contained the LeX (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The increase in mass of OVA-LeX corresponded to the addition of two LeX molecules per OVA molecule.
source: This increase corresponded to the addition of two LeX molecules per OVA molecule.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from mass spectrometry data.

claim: Native OVA does not carry any ligands for MGL1.
source: Unconjugated OVA does not carry any ligands for MGL1.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data showing lack of MGL1-Fc binding to native OVA in Figure 1B.

claim: Modification of OVA with LeX did not alter the ability to bind to MR.
source: Modification of OVA with LeX did not alter the ability to bind to MR as illustrated by equal binding kinetics of MR-Fc to native OVA and OVA-LeX.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data showing equal MR-Fc binding to OVA and OVA-LeX in Figure 1B.

claim: The conjugation of LeX to OVA conferred high-avidity binding to MGL1.
source: While native OVA interacted with the MR (MR-Fc, Figure 1B) and as earlier described (Burgdorf et al., 2007), the conjugation of LeX to OVA conferred high-avidity binding to MGL1 as revealed using the soluble recombinant form of MGL1 (MGL1-Fc, Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data showing MGL1-Fc binding to OVA-LeX in Figure 1B.

claim: MGL is expressed on both splenic and bone marrow-derived DC of C57BL/6 mice.
source: Since DC are crucial for priming of naive T cells, we first established the presence of MGL on both splenic and bone marrow-derived DC (spDCs and BM-DCs) of C57BL/6 mice by staining with the anti-MGL antibody ER-MP23 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MGL1 is expressed in wild type CD11c+ DCs.
source: Since the ER-MP23 antibody does not discriminate between the two murine MGL homologues MGL1 and MGL2, MGL1 expression in wild type (WT) CD11c+ DCs was confirmed using qRT-PCR (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Immunization of mice with OVA-LeX mixed with agonistic anti-CD40 antibodies resulted in enhanced priming of OVA-specific CD8+ T cells compared to native OVA.
source: Immunization of mice with OVA-LeX mixed with agonistic anti-CD40 antibodies resulted in the enhanced priming of OVA-specific CD8+ T cells as revealed from both higher numbers of OVA/H-2Kb tetramer binding CD8+ T cells and OVA-specific IFN-γ and TNF-producing CD8+ T cells than obtained with native OVA (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo immunization data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: MGL1 is the prime lectin involved in boosting the generation of antigen-specific effector T cells.
source: Using MGL1KO mice, that lack MGL1 expression on DC (Figure 2B), we ascertained that MGL1 is the prime lectin involved in boosting the generation of antigen-specific effector T cells as upon immunization of these mice with LeX-conjugated OVA no enhanced frequencies of OVA-specific IFN-γ and TNFα-double-producing T cells were detected (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from MGL1 KO mice immunization experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: OVA-LeX immunized MGL1 KO mice displayed comparable numbers of effector T cells as WT mice immunized with native OVA.
source: In fact, the OVA-LeX immunized MGL1 KO mice displayed comparable numbers of effector T cells as WT mice immunized with native OVA.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from MGL1 KO mice immunization experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The conjugation of two LeX glycans on OVA re-directs OVA to the CLR MGL1 and thereby enhances CD8+ T cell priming in vivo.
source: Together, these data show that the conjugation of two LeX glycans on OVA re-directs OVA to the CLR MGL1 and thereby enhances CD8+ T cell priming in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined data showing MGL1-dependent enhancement of CD8+ T cell priming.

claim: OVA-LeX-loaded and native OVA-loaded spDCs induced CD4+ OT-II T cell proliferation to a similar extent.
source: Both OVA-LeX-loaded and native OVA-loaded spDCs induced CD4+ OT-II T cell proliferation to a similar extent (Figure 3A), illustrating that the altered antigen uptake mediated by LeX did not affect loading on MHC class II molecules.
evidence: The claim is supported by T cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The altered antigen uptake mediated by LeX did not affect loading on MHC class II molecules.
source: Both OVA-LeX-loaded and native OVA-loaded spDCs induced CD4+ OT-II T cell proliferation to a similar extent (Figure 3A), illustrating that the altered antigen uptake mediated by LeX did not affect loading on MHC class II molecules.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similar T cell proliferation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Co-cultures containing OVA-LeX loaded BM-DCs or spDCs contained significantly more IFN-γ-producing T cells than those containing OVA-loaded DCs.
source: Co-cultures containing OVA-LeX loaded BM-DCs or spDCs contained significantly more IFN-γ-producing T cells than those containing OVA-loaded DCs (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing IFN-γ production in Figure 3B.

claim: Neither induction of IL-4- nor IL-17A-producing CD4+ T cells was observed with OVA-LeX loaded DCs.
source: Neither induction of IL-4- nor IL-17A-producing CD4+ T cells was observed (Figure 3B, upper and middle panel and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Induction of Foxp3+ T cells was not detected with OVA-LeX loaded DCs.
source: In addition, induction of Foxp3+ T cells was not detected (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data not shown in the manuscript.

claim: Naive OVA-specific CD4+ T cells from DO11.10 Tg mice that were stimulated with OVA-loaded BM-DCs differentiated into IL-4 secreting T cells.
source: We observed that naive OVA-specific CD4+ T cells from DO11.10 Tg mice that were stimulated with OVA-loaded BM-DCs differentiated into IL-4 secreting T cells (Figure 3B, lower panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The generation of IL-4-producing T cells was not influenced by loading DCs with OVA-LeX in BALB/c mice.
source: However, the generation of IL-4-producing T cells was not influenced by loading DCs with OVA-LeX as these cultures contained comparable percentages of IL-4-producing DO11.10 T cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: OVA-LeX-pulsed DCs induced considerably more IFN-γ-producing CD4+ T cells than native OVA-pulsed DCs using Th2-prone T cells.
source: Using these Th2-prone T cells, OVA-LeX-pulsed DCs still induced considerably more IFN-γ-producing CD4+ T cells than native OVA-pulsed DCs (Figure 3B, lower panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The amount of proliferation of OVA-specific CD4+ T cells induced by stimulation with OVA-LeX-loaded DCs after 6 days is similar to that induced by OVA-loaded DCs.
source: However we found that the amount of proliferation of OVA-specific CD4+ T cells induced by stimulation with OVA-LeX-loaded DCs after 6 days is similar to that induced by OVA-loaded DCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The augmented induction of CD4+ Th1 cells was observed in vivo with OVA-LeX immunization.
source: The augmented induction of CD4+ Th1 cells was also observed in vivo as revealed from the higher frequencies of IFN-γ-producing OVA-specific CD4+ T cells in the spleens of OVA-LeX immunized mice than in mice immunized with native OVA (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo immunization data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The increased numbers of Th1 cells induced by OVA-LeX-loaded DC are probably due to MGL1-mediated signaling.
source: These data indicate that the increased numbers of Th1 cells induced by OVA-LeX-loaded DC are not due to increased proliferation of OT-II cells, but probably due to MGL1-mediated signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing increased Th1 cells without increased proliferation.

claim: The internalization of OVA by BM-DC was significantly increased when OVA was modified with LeX.
source: The internalization of OVA by BM-DC was significantly increased when OVA was modified with LeX (Figure 4A—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing antigen uptake in Figure 4A—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both BM-DCs and spDCs induced substantially more proliferation of OT-I T cells when they were pulsed with OVA-LeX compared to native OVA.
source: Strikingly, both BM-DCs as well as spDCs induced substantially more proliferation of OT-I T cells when they were pulsed with OVA-LeX compared to native OVA (Figure 4B—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by T cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4B—figure supplement 2.

claim: At low concentrations of antigen (7.5 µg/ml), the proliferating OT-I T cells were doubled (26.7% to 51.7%) using OVA-LeX compared to using OVA.
source: Even at low concentrations of antigen (i.e. 7.5 µg/ml), the proliferating OT-I T cells were doubled (26.7% to 51.7%) using OVA-LeX compared to using OVA (Figure 4B), indicating that the modification of OVA with LeX greatly affected the cross-presentation of OVA.
evidence: The claim is supported by T cell proliferation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The modification of OVA with LeX greatly affected the cross-presentation of OVA.
source: Even at low concentrations of antigen (i.e. 7.5 µg/ml), the proliferating OT-I T cells were doubled (26.7% to 51.7%) using OVA-LeX compared to using OVA (Figure 4B), indicating that the modification of OVA with LeX greatly affected the cross-presentation of OVA.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the T cell proliferation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Detection of SIINFEKL/H-2Kb complexes on the cell membrane of OVA-LeX-loaded DCs confirmed enhanced antigen loading on MHC-I molecules compared to native OVA.
source: Moreover, detection of SIINFEKL/H-2Kb complexes on the cell membrane of OVA-LeX-loaded DCs by staining with the 25.1D1 antibody confirmed enhanced antigen loading on MHC-I molecules and transportation to the cell-surface of internalized OVA-LeX compared to native OVA (Figure 4C + Figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data using 25.1D1 antibody staining shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cross-presentation of OVA-LeX was clearly mediated by MGL1.
source: Cross-presentation of OVA-LeX was clearly mediated by MGL1 as demonstrated using MGL1 KO BM-DCs or steady-state spDCs (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from MGL1 KO mice experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cross-presentation of OVA via the MR was shown previously to be dependent on TLR signaling and the presence of high amounts of antigen.
source: Cross-presentation of OVA via the MR was shown previously to be dependent on TLR signaling and the presence of high amounts of antigen ([Burgdorf et al., 2006; Burgdorf et al., 2008; Blander and Medzhitov, 2006] and Figure 4—figure supplement 4, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The observed differences in cross-presentation between OVA and OVA-LeX were not due to any potential contamination with the TLR4 ligand LPS.
source: The observed differences in cross-presentation between OVA and OVA-LeX were not due to any potential contamination with the TLR4 ligand LPS, as both protein preparations did not trigger IL-8 production by TLR4-transfected HEK293 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from TLR4-transfected HEK293 cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Both OVA preparations neither induced maturation of BM-DCs nor altered their cytokine production.
source: In addition, both OVA preparations neither induced maturation of BM-DCs nor altered their cytokine production (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data not shown in the manuscript.

claim: MyD88/TRIF DKO BM-DCs still induced more OT-I proliferation when targeted with OVA-LeX than with OVA.
source: However, MyD88/TRIF DKO BM-DCs still induced more OT-I proliferation when targeted with OVA-LeX than with OVA (Figure 4E) and only a slight reduction of cross-presentation was observed compared to that induced by WT BM-DCs, suggesting a minor role for MyD88- or TRIF-signaling in MGL1-induced cross-presentation.
evidence: The claim is supported by T cell proliferation data from MyD88/TRIF DKO mice shown in Figure 4E.

claim: There is a minor role for MyD88- or TRIF-signaling in MGL1-induced cross-presentation.
source: However, MyD88/TRIF DKO BM-DCs still induced more OT-I proliferation when targeted with OVA-LeX than with OVA (Figure 4E) and only a slight reduction of cross-presentation was observed compared to that induced by WT BM-DCs, suggesting a minor role for MyD88- or TRIF-signaling in MGL1-induced cross-presentation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing only slight reduction in cross-presentation in MyD88/TRIF DKO mice.

claim: Neither exogenous loading of MHC-I molecules with OVA257-264 peptides nor MHC class II presentation of OVA-LeX and OVA was dependent on MyD88- or TRIF- signaling.
source: In line with previous findings, neither exogenous loading of MHC-I molecules with OVA257-264 peptides (Figure 4E) nor MHC class II presentation of OVA-LeX and OVA was dependent on MyD88- or TRIF- signaling and resulted in comparable expansion of OVA-specific T cells (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and additional data not shown.

claim: Cross-presentation induced by OVA-LeX was not reduced by the absence of TAP.
source: Surprisingly, cross-presentation induced by OVA-LeX was not reduced by the absence of TAP as OT-I proliferation induced by OVA-LeX-loaded TAP1 KO BM-DCs was not decreased compared to OVA-LeX-loaded WT BM-DC (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by T cell proliferation data from TAP1 KO mice shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The administration of OVA with LPS is cross-presented in a TAP-dependent manner.
source: In accordance with previous publications (Burgdorf et al., 2008), we showed that the administration of OVA with LPS is cross-presented in a TAP-dependent manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and citation to previous work.

claim: The presentation of exogenously loaded OVA257-264 peptide is equal by both WT and TAP1 KO BM-DCs.
source: Furthermore, the possibility that the results are confounded by reduced levels of MHC-class I on TAP1 KOBM-DCs were excluded as the presentation of exogenously loaded OVA257-264 peptide is equal by both WT and TAP1 KOBM-DCs (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cross-presentation of OVA-LeX by BM-DCs from Cathepsin-S KO mice was not reduced compared to WT BM-DCs.
source: In addition, we excluded the involvement of the Cathepsin-S pathway for cross-presentation of OVA-LeX as cross-presentation of OVA-LeX by BM-DCs from Cathepsin-S KO mice (Cat-S KO) was not reduced compared to WT BM-DCs (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by T cell proliferation data from Cat-S KO mice shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The MHC-class II-restricted CD4+ T cell proliferation was compromised in the Cat-S KO BM-DCs.
source: As expected, the MHC-class II-restricted CD4+ T cell proliferation was compromised in the Cat-S KO BM-DCs (data not shown), illustrating the involvement of Cathepsin-S in cleaving the invariant chain of the MHC-class II molecule (Nakagawa et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data not shown and citation to previous work.

claim: OVA-LeX co-localized with EEA1 and Rab11 at 15 min with high co-localization scores.
source: Co-staining with markers for early endosomal (EEA-1), late endosomal/lysosomal (LAMP1) and recycling endosomal (Rab11) compartments illustrated a swift co-localization of OVA-LeX with EEA1 and Rab11 as shown by high co-localization scores at 15 min (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The co-localization of OVA-LeX with EEA1 and Rab11 was strongly decreased at 60 min.
source: However, this co-localization score was strongly decreased at 60 min.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At 60 min, higher co-localization scores were detected for OVA-LeX with LAMP1 and Rab11.
source: At this time-point, higher co-localization scores were detected for OVA-LeX with LAMP1 and Rab11 (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Native OVA, which internalized via MR, was routed to EEA1+Rab11+ compartments within 2h.
source: We confirmed that native OVA, which internalized via MR, was routed to EEA1+Rab11+ compartments within 2h (Figure 6C, upper-left panel and [Burgdorf et al., 2008]).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6C and citation to previous work.

claim: The neoglycosylation with LeX altered the intracellular routing of OVA, showing its presence predominantly within LAMP1+Rab11+ compartments.
source: However, the neoglycosylation with LeX altered the intracellular routing of OVA, showing its presence predominantly within LAMP1+Rab11+ compartments (Figure 6C, upper-right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: OVA-LeX internalized by BM-DC from MGL1 KO mice was routed to EEA1+Rab11+ compartments and did not end up in LAMP1+Rab11+ compartments.
source: Moreover, OVA-LeX internalized by BM-DC from MGL1 KO mice was routed to EEA1+Rab11+ compartments and did not end up in LAMP1+Rab11+ compartments, similar to OVA in WT BM-DC (Figure 6C, lower panels + Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Upon internalization, OVA-LeX is rapidly shuttled to Rab11+EEA1+ compartments from where it moves to Rab11+LAMP1+ compartments, where it persists for longer periods (>24h).
source: Together, these data suggest that upon internalization, OVA-LeX is rapidly shuttled to Rab11+EEA1+ compartments from where it moves to Rab11+LAMP1+ compartments, where it persists for longer periods (i.e. >24h).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the imaging data showing temporal changes in co-localization.

claim: Internalization via MGL1 allows the antigen to enter the endosomal/lysosomal pathway.
source: Thus, these results indicate that internalization via MGL1 allows the antigen to enter the endosomal/lysosomal pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing routing to LAMP1+ compartments.

claim: MGL1 starts dissociating from LeX already at pH 6.5.
source: MGL1 starts dissociating from LeX already at pH 6.5 (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data showing pH-dependent binding shown in Figure 6D.

claim: OVA-LeX becomes available for degradation in the early and late endosomal compartments.
source: This indicates that OVA-LeX becomes available for degradation in the early and late endosomal compartments, compartments both associated with cross-presentation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the pH dissociation data and knowledge about compartment pH.

claim: Even two days after antigen pulse, OVA-LeX-loaded DC induced strong expansion of OT-I T cells.
source: Indeed, even two days after antigen pulse, OVA-LeX-loaded DC induced strong expansion of OT-I T cells, suggesting that OVA-LeX-loaded DC have prolonged cross-presentation capacity (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by T cell proliferation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: OVA-LeX-loaded DC have prolonged cross-presentation capacity.
source: Indeed, even two days after antigen pulse, OVA-LeX-loaded DC induced strong expansion of OT-I T cells, suggesting that OVA-LeX-loaded DC have prolonged cross-presentation capacity (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing sustained T cell proliferation after 48h.

claim: At the highest antigen concentration used (30 µg/ml), the percentage of proliferated OT-I T cells was only slightly reduced 48 h after pulse compared to that induced by DCs that were pulsed with OVA-LeX for 4 h.
source: At the highest antigen concentration used (i.e. 30 µg/ml), the percentage of proliferated OT-I T cells was only slightly reduced 48 h after pulse compared to that induced by DCs that were pulsed with OVA-LeX for 4 h (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by T cell proliferation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Expansion of OT-I T cells driven by 48 h pulse loaded DCs was even detectable at low antigen concentrations (3.75 µg/ml).
source: Expansion of OT-I T cells driven by 48 h pulse loaded DCs was even detectable at low antigen concentrations (3.75 µg/ml).
evidence: The claim is supported by T cell proliferation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: OT-II proliferation induced by DCs pulsed with OVA-LeX for 48h was still detectable although less pronounced than the OT-I induced proliferation.
source: OT-II proliferation induced by DCs pulsed with OVA-LeX for 48h was also still detectable although less pronounced than the OT-I induced proliferation (Figure 7B), suggesting that the prolonged storage of antigen in these intracellular compartments predominantly favored cross-presentation.
evidence: The claim is supported by T cell proliferation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The prolonged storage of antigen in Rab11+LAMP1+ compartments predominantly favored cross-presentation.
source: OT-II proliferation induced by DCs pulsed with OVA-LeX for 48h was also still detectable although less pronounced than the OT-I induced proliferation (Figure 7B), suggesting that the prolonged storage of antigen in these intracellular compartments predominantly favored cross-presentation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing stronger OT-I than OT-II proliferation after 48h.

claim: Antigen internalized by MGL1 is routed from Rab11+EEA1+ compartments towards Rab11+LAMP1+ compartments, which seem to associate with the extended antigen-processing and cross-presentation.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that antigen internalized by MGL1 is routed from RAb11+EEA1+ compartments towards Rab11+LAMP1+ compartments, which seem to associate with the extended antigen-processing and cross-presentation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined imaging and functional data.

claim: The glycosylation-profile of antigens has a major influence on antigen uptake and intracellular compartmentalization.
source: We here demonstrate that the glycosylation-profile of antigens has a major influence on antigen uptake and intracellular compartmentalization, thereby affecting both antigen presentation and the type and strength of the induced immune response.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Modification of OVA with LeX glycans directs OVA towards MGL1, skewing naive CD4+ T cell differentiation towards IFNγ-producing Th1 cells.
source: Modification of the model-antigen OVA with LeX glycans directs OVA towards MGL1, skewing naive CD4+ T cell differentiation towards IFNγ-producing Th1 cells.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined experimental data showing MGL1-dependent Th1 skewing.

claim: Targeting OVA to MGL1 through the conjugation of LeX substantially enhanced cross-presentation as revealed by the increased frequency of OVA-specific CD8+ effector T cells in vitro and in vivo.
source: Moreover, targeting OVA to MGL1 through the conjugation of LeX, substantially enhanced cross-presentation as revealed by the increased frequency of OVA-specific CD8+ effector T cells in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined in vitro and in vivo experimental data.

claim: MGL1-dependent cross-presentation occurred at low antigen dose and independently of TLR-signaling.
source: Importantly, MGL1-dependent cross-presentation occurred at low antigen dose and independently of TLR-signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data from MyD88/TRIF DKO mice and low-dose experiments.

claim: MGL1-mediated cross-presentation did not involve TAP-transporters and Cathepsin-S.
source: Moreover, this cross-presentation pathway did not involve TAP-transporters and Cathepsin-S.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data from TAP1 KO and Cat-S KO mice.

claim: MGL1 targeting involved antigen routing to a Rab11+LAMP1+ compartment in which antigen was present for prolonged periods.
source: MGL1 targeting involved antigen routing to a Rab11+LAMP1+ compartment in which antigen was present for prolonged periods.
evidence: The claim is based on the imaging and functional data showing prolonged antigen presence.

claim: Previous studies on CLR-mediated antigen uptake and cross-presentation, in particular by the MR, demonstrated a clear requirement for a TLR ligand.
source: Previous studies on CLR-mediated antigen uptake and cross-presentation, in particular by the MR, demonstrated a clear requirement for a TLR ligand (Kovacsovics-Bankowski and Rock, 1995; Burgdorf et al., 2008; Sancho et al., 2008; Segura et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The addition of LeX glycans to OVA obviates the need for TLR signals for the induction of cross-presentation and Th1 priming in vitro.
source: The fact that the addition of LeX glycans to OVA obviates the need for TLR signals for the induction of cross-presentation and Th1 priming in vitro, may indicate that MGL1 signaling is involved in these processes.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data from MyD88/TRIF DKO mice.

claim: Some CLR, like DC-SIGN, Clec9A and Dectin-1 are known to induce signaling after triggering by their natural ligands.
source: Some CLR, like DC-SIGN, Clec9A and Dectin-1 are known to induce signaling after triggering by their natural ligands (Geijtenbeek and Gringhuis, 2009; Sancho et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: No signaling pathway has been described for MGL1.
source: Till now, no signaling pathway has been described for MGL1.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the existing literature at the time of publication.

claim: Triggering of huMGL resulted in ERK1/2 and NF-κB activation, and results in elevated levels of IL-10 and TNF.
source: Triggering of huMGL resulted in ERK1/2 and NF-κB activation, and results in elevated levels of IL-10 and TNF (Li et al., 2012; van Vliet et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The uptake of LeX-modified OVA through MGL1 was not associated with any DC maturation or altered cytokine production by DCs.
source: In our studies, the uptake of LeX-modified OVA through MGL1 was not associated with any DC maturation or altered cytokine production by DCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data mentioned in the text.

claim: OVA-LeX induced an enhanced frequency of Th1 cells in vitro and of antigen-specific effector T cells in vivo when combined with agonistic anti-CD40 Abs.
source: The fact that OVA-LeX induced an enhanced frequency of Th1 cells in vitro and of antigen-specific effector T cells in vivo when combined with agonistic anti-CD40 Abs illustrates that a yet to be determined costimulatory signal is essential for the induction of effector CD8+ and CD4+ T cells.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data from in vitro and in vivo experiments.

claim: A yet to be determined costimulatory signal is essential for the induction of effector CD8+ and CD4+ T cells by OVA-LeX.
source: The fact that OVA-LeX induced an enhanced frequency of Th1 cells in vitro and of antigen-specific effector T cells in vivo when combined with agonistic anti-CD40 Abs illustrates that a yet to be determined costimulatory signal is essential for the induction of effector CD8+ and CD4+ T cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the requirement for anti-CD40 antibodies.

claim: The powerful function of MGL1 to establish antigen-specific immunity stands opposite to its recently demonstrated anti-inflammatory function.
source: This powerful function of MGL1 to establish antigen-specific immunity, stands opposite to its recently demonstrated anti-inflammatory function, which include induction of IL-10 production and altered adhesive function by APC (Saba et al., 2009; Westcott et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the current findings and citations to previous work.

claim: The 'cytosolic pathway' of cross-presentation allows receptor-mediated endocytosis or phagocytosis and antigen translocation into the cytosol, where they are degraded into antigenic peptides by the proteasome and transported into the lumen of the ER or ER/phagosomal fusion compartments by TAP-transporters.
source: The 'cytosolic pathway' of cross-presentation allows receptor-mediated endocytosis or phagocytosis and antigen translocation into the cytosol, where they are degraded into antigenic peptides by the proteasome and transported into the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Kovacsovics-Bankowski and Rock, 1995; Shen et al., 2004) or ER/phagosomal fusion compartments (Guermonprez et al., 2003; Houde et al., 2003) by TAP-transporters.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work describing the cytosolic pathway.

claim: Soluble OVA is taken up via the MR and is supplied to stable early endosomal compartments where the MHC class I machinery and TAP-transporters are selectively recruited.
source: A variation to the cytosolic pathway was described in which soluble OVA is taken up via the MR and is supplied to stable early endosomal compartments (Burgdorf et al., 2007). In these compartments, the MHC class I machinery as well as TAP-transporters are selectively recruited, facilitating direct loading of antigen-derived peptides onto MHC class I molecules without trafficking to the ER.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Burgdorf et al., 2007.

claim: The 'vacuolar pathway' allows antigens to be degraded into peptides in early endosomal compartments by endosomal proteases like Cathepsin-S, to be loaded on MHC class I molecules in the same compartment, thus is TAP-independent.
source: The 'vacuolar pathway' allows antigens to be degraded into peptides in early endosomal compartments by endosomal proteases like Cathepsin-S, to be loaded on MHC class I molecules in the same compartment, thus is TAP-independent (Shen et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work describing the vacuolar pathway.

claim: The MGL1 cross-presentation pathway is different than that of the MR and may occur via antigen storage compartments similar to those described for FcγR-targeted antigens.
source: Our data indicate that the MGL1 cross-presentation pathway is different than that of the MR and may occur via antigen storage compartments similar to those described for FcγR-targeted antigens (van Montfoort et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: Rab11 activity mediates delivery of MHC-I molecules to phagosomes used for cross-presentation during infection.
source: It is tempting to speculate that in these compartments cross-presentation of OVA is facilitated by Rab11 as it was recently shown that Rab11 activity mediates delivery of MHC-I molecules to phagosomes used for cross-presentation during infection (Nair-Gupta et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Nair-Gupta et al., 2014.

source: The prolonged antigen cross-presentation via MGL1 allows sustained cross-priming of CD8+ T cells in vivo and thus the efficacy of tumor vaccines that target MGL1 may be higher than of conventional vaccines containing non-targeted antigens.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing prolonged cross-presentation.

claim: Multivalent presentation of LeX may alter avidity-induced MGL-1 signaling and antigen presentation, and induce an anti-inflammatory immune repertoire.
source: Although in our studies only two LeX glycans were conjugated to each OVA molecule, it cannot be ruled out that multivalent presentation of LeX, such as often observed on tumors or pathogens (Bergman et al., 2004; Saeland and van, 2011), may alter avidity-induced MGL-1 signaling and antigen presentation, and induce an anti-inflammatory immune repertoire.
evidence: The claim is speculative, acknowledging uncertainty about the effects of multivalent LeX presentation.

claim: Conjugation of LeX to tumor-antigens could be beneficial for the induction of potent anti-tumor responses.
source: The fact that pulsing of DCs with OVA-LeX resulted in improved cross-priming and Th1-skewing indicates that conjugation of these carbohydrates to tumor-antigens could be beneficial for the induction of potent anti-tumor responses.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and speculation about therapeutic applications.

source: In conclusion, our studies indicate that the glycan composition of protein antigens is of fundamental importance in dictating the intracellular routing and Th-skewing, and should be considered as a major determinant in the design of therapeutic vaccines against cancer and infectious diseases.
